opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly one I think about a lot, because there's a real gap between an abstraction being *useful for compression* and it actually carving nature at its joints.

The first test I'd reach for is intervention. If a library of abstractions has picked up something causal, the system should be able to predict what happens when you change one part of the world while leaving everything else alone. A purely correlational abstraction tends to break under that kind of manipulation. A causal one keeps working, because it encodes the mechanism and not just the regularities that happened to show up in the training data. So you'd set up environments, ideally interactive ones, and check whether the synthesized programs give correct counterfactual predictions after you intervene on a variable.

The second test is transfer under distribution shift. What I like about programs is that they're compositional. If you learned a concept like "support" or "containment" as a real piece of causal structure, you should be able to recombine it with other concepts in configurations you never saw, and it should still make the right predictions. If performance collapses as soon as the surface statistics change, that's a strong sign the abstraction latched onto a shortcut.

The third is sample efficiency on new tasks. A good causal abstraction should make learning downstream things dramatically easier. If adding a concept to the library means the system can now solve a whole family of new problems from just a few examples, that's evidence it captured something structurally real. If it only helps on problems that look like the ones it came from, I'd be more skeptical.

Then there's a more qualitative check that I think is underrated: inspect the programs. One big advantage of the symbolic approach is that you can read what was learned. You can ask whether the abstraction matches how a scientist or a person would describe the mechanism, and whether its parameters mean something physically. Interpretability won't prove causality, but it does let you notice when something is obviously wrong.

I'd add one caveat. You can't fully verify causal structure from passive observation alone. That's a basic lesson from the causality literature. So I think the most compelling version of this research has the learner act in the world: run its own experiments, build hypotheses as programs, and revise them when its predictions fail. That's much closer to how children and scientists do it, and it's where I think program synthesis is especially well suited, because a program is a hypothesis you can actually test.

r001.rationale: The response proposes interactive environments where the learner intervenes on variables and checks whether its programs correctly predict the results.

r002.rationale: It contrasts causal abstractions with correlational shortcuts, but does not explain that equivalent descriptions of the same function space can make function learning alone insufficient to identify the right abstractions.

r003.rationale: It does not state that a program synthesis library’s current lack of usefulness would fail to falsify the library.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that most of the tests we actually run don't get at causality at all. They get at compression. When we do library learning, say in DreamCoder, the metric is something like: does the learned library make the training programs shorter, and does it let us solve more held-out tasks faster? That's a statistical notion of a good abstraction. It tells you the abstraction is useful for prediction or for search, but it doesn't tell you the abstraction corresponds to a mechanism in the world.

So if I wanted to test for causal content specifically, I'd lean on the thing that distinguishes causal knowledge from correlational knowledge, which is intervention. You have a learned library of abstractions, and the question is whether they are the right joints to intervene on. The experiment I'd want is something like this: build a world, a simulator, where you know the true generative process, and you know which variables are the actual causal levers. Let the system learn abstractions from observations of that world. Then don't score it on reconstruction or held-out likelihood. Score it on whether the primitives it invents line up with the levers. If you reach into the environment and change one causal factor, does that change map onto editing one argument of one learned function, or does it smear out across a dozen unrelated pieces of the program? That locality of edits is, to me, the signature of an abstraction that has captured something causal rather than merely something compressive.

A second test is transfer under distribution shift, but a specific kind of shift. If you train on a world and then change the distribution over inputs but leave the mechanisms intact, a causal abstraction should survive. A merely statistical one often won't. Conversely, if you change a mechanism, the system should have to relearn exactly the piece of the library that corresponds to it and nothing else. So you can almost use the pattern of what breaks as a diagnostic.

The third thing, and this is where I think program synthesis has a real advantage over end-to-end neural models, is that the abstractions are inspectable. You can take a learned function, hand it to a person, and ask: does this correspond to a concept you'd use to explain the world? That's not rigorous in the way an interventional test is, but it's a kind of face validity that you simply can't get from a weight matrix. And in the domains we've worked in, things like simple physics or drawing or list manipulation, you do sometimes see the system reinvent things like "repeat this motion n times" or "apply a force then let it settle," which look like causal structure rather than surface regularity.

The caveat I'd put on all of this is that compression and causality are not independent. Part of why we think a minimum-description-length kind of objective is a reasonable proxy is that the true causal structure of a world usually is the shortest explanation of it. But "usually" is doing a lot of work there, and I think the interventional tests are how you find out when it fails.

r001.rationale: The response proposes intervening on causal factors in a simulator and checking whether each intervention maps locally to an edit in a learned function.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss equivalent descriptions of the same function space or explain why function learning alone cannot identify the right abstractions.

r003.rationale: It does not state that a program synthesis library’s current lack of usefulness would fail to falsify it.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish an abstraction that compresses your observations from one that actually supports interventions. If I discover a little program that explains a dataset very well, that’s interesting, but it doesn’t by itself tell me that the program describes the causal structure of the world. There could be several programs that fit those observations and disagree about what happens when you change something.

So I would take those disagreements seriously and use them to design experiments. Ask the learned program to predict what will happen if we intervene on a particular variable or change part of the environment. Then perform that intervention and see whether the prediction holds. Ideally, you’d choose interventions that distinguish competing explanations, rather than just collect more examples where they all agree.

I’d also test whether the abstraction transfers to new situations where the same proposed mechanism operates, but the surrounding correlations are different. Can you reuse it without having to relearn everything? That would be evidence that you’ve captured something stable about the process.

But I’d be careful about treating successful transfer as proof of causality. The strongest case would come from a combination of predictive success under interventions, transfer across environments, and explicit comparison with alternative explanations. Program synthesis gives you a language for stating those explanations precisely; the experiments still have to tell you which ones are right.

r001.rationale: It proposes predicting outcomes of interventions and then performing them in the environment to test whether the learned program’s predictions hold.

r002.rationale: It notes that multiple programs may fit the observations and disagree about interventions, but does not explain that equivalent descriptions of the same function space can keep function learning alone from identifying the right abstractions.

r003.rationale: It does not address whether a program synthesis library’s current lack of usefulness would falsify it.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by separating two claims. One is that an abstraction helps you compress a set of programs or solve tasks more efficiently. The other is that it corresponds to something causal in the world. The first doesn’t establish the second.

To test the causal claim, you need interventions. Suppose a system learns an abstraction for how an object moves. Can you change the object’s mass, change the surface, or apply a force, and have the abstraction predict what happens? Crucially, you’d want to hold out some of those interventions during learning. Otherwise, it might just be summarizing patterns it’s already seen.

I’d also ask whether the abstraction supports transfer. If you change one part of the environment, can the system adapt by changing one corresponding part of its program, while retaining the rest? That would be evidence that it has identified a useful mechanism.

And you need comparisons with alternative abstractions that explain the observational data equally well. Can interventions distinguish them? Program synthesis gives you explicit hypotheses you can inspect and execute, which is helpful. But being a program doesn’t make a hypothesis causal. The evidence comes from whether it survives those experimental tests.

r001.rationale: It proposes changing properties of the environment and holding out interventions to test whether an abstraction predicts outcomes and captures a mechanism.

r002.rationale: It mentions alternative abstractions that explain observational data equally well, but does not explain that equivalent descriptions of the same function space can keep function learning alone from identifying the right abstraction.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that a program synthesis library’s current lack of usefulness would not falsify it.
